title: Retry the intent
lesson: Preserve one operation key and its arguments when an agent retries a lost response; reject changed intent rather than silently repeating or changing the effect.
limitations: Illustrative in-house ticket tool: key record and ticket share one database transaction; not a commercial tracker feature claim.
Assumes valid permissions and retained keys; concurrent calls, expiry, and external effects require the guide and service-specific tests.
Audio was analysed for level and synchronization but not physically listened to.
Self-reviewed by gpt-6-astra; no independent comparative ranking or default-cut promotion.

transcript.text: A release agent asks an illustrative ticket tool to create a ticket for release v1 using operation key k7. One database commit saves both ticket #47 and the key-to-ticket record; the count becomes one.
The reply carrying ticket #47 is lost. The agent does not know the outcome, but the database still contains the ticket. The runner prepares another attempt with the same key and release data.
The retry looks up k7 and returns the existing ticket #47. No second write occurs, and the agent receives the identifier while the ticket count stays at one.
The caller changes the release data to v2 while keeping k7. This tool’s contract detects a parameter mismatch and rejects the request; it neither changes ticket #47 nor creates another ticket.
The unchanged v1 ticket and count of one remain in focus, then the scene fades. This illustrates a service-enforced contract; an agent prompt alone does not supply persistence or permissions.
